what_it_does: Training a large language model to be helpful and safe (a process called Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, or RLHF) requires four separate AI models running in a complicated dance of generate-then-evaluate-then-update steps, but today's systems use the same rigid setup for all of them, leaving GPUs sitting idle much of the time. REAL fixes this by reshuffling which model lives on which GPUs at each step — a technique called parameter reallocation — so every step uses the parallelism setup that actually fits its workload. The result is up to 3.58x more training throughput compared to leading open-source RLHF systems.
method_in_detail:
The idea. When you train a large language model with RLHF, you run four models per iteration: an Actor (the model being trained) that generates text, a Reward model that scores the text, a Reference model that keeps the Actor from going off the rails, and a Critic model that estimates future reward. Each has a very different job — generation is slow and sequential, scoring is a quick forward pass, training involves heavy backward-pass math. Yet existing systems lock all four models into one fixed way of splitting work across GPUs for the entire training run.

How it works. REAL treats each model function call (generate, score, train) as an independent unit. Before training starts, a search engine considers every plausible assignment of GPU subsets and split strategies — how many ways to slice layers across machines (pipeline parallelism), how many ways to split a single layer's matrix math (tensor parallelism), how many independent data copies to run (data parallelism). For a 64-GPU cluster this is over 10^16 possible combinations, so REAL uses a randomized search called Metropolis-Hastings (a technique from statistical physics that accepts worse answers occasionally to escape local traps) guided by a fast time estimator. The estimator profiles individual layer timings in a few minutes and then predicts full-plan cost in microseconds.

The key design choice. When the Actor switches from generating text (best served by heavy tensor parallelism to reduce per-step latency) to training (best served by more pipeline stages and less cross-GPU chatter), REAL physically moves the model weights across the GPU cluster to adopt the new layout. This weight transfer is overlapped with other work and costs only a few percent of total time.

The catch. The search assumes predictable, stable workloads. If generation lengths vary wildly (very common in practice), cost estimates become inaccurate. REAL also cannot guarantee it finds the globally best plan, only a very good one.

The result. On LLaMA models from 7B to 70B parameters across 8 to 128 NVIDIA H100 GPUs, REAL reaches up to 3.58x higher throughput than DeepSpeed-Chat, OpenRLHF, and NeMo-Aligner, and 54-81% higher than a hand-tuned Megatron-inspired baseline — with the gap widening at longer context lengths.
